## QUESTION

1. __Take time to get to know your data.__ Based on some initial exploration, identify 3 variables in the dataset you think will have strong predictive ability for determining if a house was built before 1980. Explain/justify the reasoning behind your guesses (for example with plots).

These three plots shows the difference in data between houses that were build after 1980 (indicated by a 0) and houses that were build before 1980 (indicated by a 1). It is very typical for a house that is build before 1980 to have only 1 story, with few outliers. It is also typical for a house build before 1980 to have fewerbathrooms, between 1 and 2 typically. And finally, homes build before 1980 tend to have a smaller average living space than those which were built after 1980.

These three variables together can help to predict whether a house was build before or after 1980 with a bit more accuracy when all used together.

```{python}
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

df = pl.read_csv("dwellings_ml.csv")

# Create a boxplot for the number of stories in a house before and after 1980.

plot_stories = df.select(["before1980", "stories"]).to_pandas()

stories_plot = (ggplot(plot_stories, aes(x="before1980", y="stories")) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
      title="Number of Stories by Construction Period",
      x="Before 1980 indicator",
      y="Number of stories"
  )
)

# Create a boxplot for the number of bathrooms in a house before and after 1980.

plot_bath = df.select(["before1980", "numbaths"]).to_pandas()

bath_plot = (ggplot(plot_bath, aes(x="before1980", y="numbaths")) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  labs(
    title="Number of Bathrooms by Construction Period",
    x="Before 1980 indicator",
    y="Number of bathrooms"
  )
)

# Create a boxplot for the living area of a house before and after 1980.

plot_area = df.select(["before1980", "livearea"]).to_pandas()

area_plot = (ggplot(plot_area, aes(x = as_discrete("before1980"), y = "livearea")) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title="Living Area by Construction Period",
    x = "Before 1980 indicator",
    y = "Living area in square feet"
  )
)

# Display all three boxplots.

display(gggrid([stories_plot, bath_plot, area_plot], ncol=3))
```

2. __Build a classification model labeling houses as being built “before 1980” or “during or after 1980”.__ Your goal is to reach or exceed 90% accuracy. Report your final model choice and any other model parameters you may have tweaked (train-test split ratio, tuning parameters, etc). 

I used a Random Forest classifer to predict if a house was built before or after 1980. Using the 3 variables identified in question 1 along with the variables for homes with a basement, quality category C and fi the home had an attached garage, I was able to reach an accuracy of 90%.

To test the model, I split the data into 80% and predicted on the remaining 20% to test the model. Additionally, the modal had 200 trees, a max depth of 15, and a minimum size of 2 per leaf. The results are also expected to be repeatable to ensure that the model is working as expected.

```{python}
import polars as pl
import numpy as np

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn import metrics
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

from pathlib import Path

homes = pl.read_csv("dwellings_ml.csv")

# Uses the three variables from Question 1, along with basement, quality_C and gartype_Att to have enough data to predict more accurately.

predictors = ["stories", "numbaths", "livearea", "basement", "quality_C", "gartype_Att"]

x = homes.select(predictors).to_numpy()
y = homes["before1980"].to_numpy()

# Reliablty trains on 80% of the homes and tests on the remaining 20%.

x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    x, 
    y,
    test_size = 0.20,
    random_state = 42,
    stratify = y
)

# The Random Forest combines predictions from many decision trees.

model = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators = 200,
    max_depth = 15,
    min_samples_leaf = 2,
    random_state = 42,
    n_jobs = -1
)

model.fit(x_train, y_train)

# Compares predicted values to actual values of the remaining 20% of homes.

predictions = model.predict(x_test)
accuracy = metrics.accuracy_score(y_test, predictions)

print(f"Test accuracy: {accuracy:.2%}")
```
